title: Yoder Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Yoder wells have a 490-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $30,500-$46,300.
h1: Yoder, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Well records within five miles of Yoder show a mostly deep Denver Basin setting. The median recorded well is 490 feet, and the middle half runs from 315 to 600 feet. That gives a buyer a more useful starting point than a single nearby well, because depth can change with the aquifer, permit conditions, and the exact lot.

Most records are for domestic or household use, and all named aquifer records are within the Denver Basin system. The data is useful for planning, but it is not a guarantee that a new hole will match a neighboring well. Before buying land, review nearby permits, water rights, septic options, and the intended use of the property.

sections.heading: Yoder’s wells are commonly deep
sections.html:
Yoder’s recorded depths center on 490 feet. The middle half of wells falls between 315 and 600 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 700 feet and the deepest record is 900 feet. Depth is not evenly distributed: 49% are between 300 and 600 feet, 28% are 600 feet or deeper, and only 7% are under 100 feet.

That spread matters when requesting a drilling bid. A driller should price the likely depth range rather than assume a shallow domestic well. Permits identify Laramie Fox Hills and Arapahoe aquifers, along with unnamed or fractured-bedrock conditions. In Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the target formation, casing, grout, access, and final water level can all affect the completed job.

sections.heading: Most Yoder wells make usable domestic quantities
sections.html:
Among Yoder-area records that report pump yield, the median is 9.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute, and 82% report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Another 14% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 4% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No recorded wells in this dataset are under 1 gallon per minute.

For a household buyer, these figures describe a generally workable production range, not a promise for a particular parcel. Yield testing, storage capacity, pump selection, and the well permit’s allowed use still matter. Most permits list domestic or household use, with stock use also common. Irrigation is uncommon in the records, so do not assume a domestic well can support large landscape demands.

sections.heading: The recorded water levels do not show a simple decline
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 315 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 220 to 385 feet. That is the water level when the well is not being pumped, not the drilled depth. A well can be 490 feet deep and still have water substantially above the bottom of the hole.

The decade comparison does not point to a steadily dropping table in these records. The median measured level was 365 feet below surface in the 2010s and 320 feet in the 2020s. Measurement methods, locations, and the mix of wells can affect that comparison, so treat it as local context rather than a forecast. Ask for the static level and pumping drawdown from any specific well.

sections.heading: Yoder permit history identifies the active drillers
sections.html:
El Paso County DWR records within five miles of Yoder contain 777 permitted wells. Of those, 503 are recorded as constructed, 526 report total depth, 359 report pump yield, and 77 report static water level. The record set extends through a newest permit year of 2025, so recent activity is represented.

Kunau Drilling Llc (Kunau, Timothy R.) appears most often, with 280 records. Hamacher Well Works Inc (Hamacher, Alan Ray) has 123, and Can America Drilling, Inc. (Arde, Wayne A.) has 65. These records show who has worked in the area, but availability, pricing, and suitability for your parcel must be confirmed directly. Check permits near Rush, Ellicott, and the surrounding eastern El Paso County area before choosing a contractor.

sections.heading: Budget roughly thirty to forty-six thousand for a finished well
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At Yoder’s 490-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $24,500 to $34,300. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $30,500 to $46,300.

Use that range for early site budgeting, not as a fixed quote. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, power distance, storage requirements, and site conditions can move the total. Ask each driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work so competing bids describe the same scope.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low yield, and the building site
sections.html:
Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about ten miles of Yoder. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped area. The PFAS locations do not establish contamination at a specific parcel, but they are a reason to review available sampling information and test a private well before relying on it for drinking water.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk cannot be eliminated by a neighborhood median. Fractured or variable formations can produce different results on nearby lots. Also confirm septic setbacks, soil suitability, driveway access, electric service, and the proposed home location before drilling. A water permit does not by itself solve every septic, building, or land-use issue.

sections.heading: Use the records before buying or building near Yoder
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s neighboring permits, then compare total depth, aquifer name, reported yield, static level, use, and construction status. The broader Yoder record suggests that a buyer should plan for a deep well rather than base expectations on the small share under 100 feet. Ask for the well construction report and pump test for any existing well, and verify that the actual use matches the permit.

For a vacant lot, have a Colorado water professional review the permit path and likely drilling interval before closing. Household wells are commonly permitted for domestic use, while stock, irrigation, and other uses may require different authorization. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be relevant. Build the septic and house layout around confirmed water, access, and soil information—not just the nearest well map.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Yoder, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Yoder is 490 feet. The middle half runs from 315 to 600 feet, 28% are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest record is 900 feet. Nearly half fall between 300 and 600 feet, so a buyer should budget for a relatively deep well rather than expect a shallow hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Yoder, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $50 to $70 per foot. At the 490-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $24,500 to $34,300. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $30,500 to $46,300. Actual bids can change with depth, access, casing, grout, power distance, and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Yoder?
faq.a: Reported well yields have a median of 9.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. Most records, 82%, fall from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Yield is not guaranteed for a new hole, so review the neighboring pump tests and plan storage and pump equipment around the tested result.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Yoder, Colorado?
faq.a: Private well water should be tested rather than assumed safe. Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about ten miles of Yoder, although those locations do not prove contamination at a particular parcel. Test an existing or new well for relevant contaminants, review nearby environmental information, and retest when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are Yoder wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple decline. Median static water level was 365 feet below surface in the 2010s and 320 feet in the 2020s. Only 77 records report static water level, and measurements vary by well and method. For a specific property, rely on its measured static level and pumping drawdown rather than the area median.
